title: How Strangers Are Feeding India's Exam Protesters Through Swiggy and Zomato
excerpt: Anonymous supporters across India and abroad are using food delivery apps to send meals to student protesters, turning digital platforms into tools of solidarity.
body:
• Anonymous supporters across India and overseas are ordering food through Swiggy, Zomato, and Zepto for delivery to exam-protest sites in Delhi, Ranchi, and other cities
  • The trend, first seen at Delhi's Jantar Mantar during the CJP-led NEET paper leak protests, has spread to Ranchi where students are demonstrating over JPSC and JSSC exam irregularities
  • The phenomenon mirrors similar cross-border digital solidarity seen in Indonesia in 2025, when people from Southeast Asian countries ordered food for protest-participating delivery riders

Across India's protest sites — from Delhi's Jantar Mantar to Ranchi's streets — a stream of Swiggy and Zomato delivery riders has been arriving with meals, snacks, and bottled water ordered by strangers. The food isn't for paying customers. It's for the students.

The practice took off during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protests at Jantar Mantar over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak. As thousands of students camped out demanding accountability from the government, anonymous individuals from across India — and even overseas — began placing orders on delivery platforms with simple instructions: distribute the food to whoever needs it.

From Samosas to 70-Pizza Orders

Pradeep Kumar Singh, a Swiggy delivery partner, told ANI that Jantar Mantar became a regular destination for these solidarity orders. "An order comes, and then the person says, 'Brother, distribute it right there; give it to whoever needs it,'" Singh said. "Yesterday, I had an order for samosas. I was told to just bring them here and distribute them."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=87gpoFOTex0

The scale quickly became staggering. One delivery rider, Neg Singh, told the Associated Press he had made 19 trips to the protest site. On one run, he picked up 70 pizzas — an order so large it took three riders to carry it through the crowds. That order came from someone in Noida, about 25 kilometres away.

"There are a lot of people that I understand might not be able to come here, but they are sending their love."

— Shakti Vashisth, 24, protester at Jantar Mantar

The support extended well beyond India's borders. Mahendra Kumar, another delivery partner, arrived at the site with tea ordered by a customer from outside the country. "They said, 'Go to Jantar Mantar and give it to the brothers,'" he told ANI. A Zomato and Zepto delivery executive described the entire arrangement as "student service."

Ranchi and Beyond: The Trend Spreads

The food delivery solidarity model has now spread to Ranchi, where students have been protesting over alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) examinations. According to India Today, strangers have begun ordering meals for Ranchi protesters through the same delivery apps, replicating the pattern first established at Delhi's Jantar Mantar.

Jharkhand's exam controversies have their own history. The BJP's youth wing clashed with police outside the JPSC office on July 22 over the 14th Combined Civil Services Preliminary Examination, alleging results were declared without publishing cut-off marks. Students in Ranchi and Hazaribagh have staged multiple protests over paper leak allegations tied to the JSSC CGL exam, which was taken by over three lakh candidates.

A Global Pattern of Digital Solidarity

India's food delivery protest support isn't without precedent. In August 2025, when protests erupted across Indonesia over cost-of-living concerns, people from Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines, and Thailand used Grab and Gojek to order food for Indonesian delivery riders participating in demonstrations. The hashtag #SEAblings went viral as cross-border solidarity played out through delivery platforms, according to the BBC.

At the CJP protest, the volume of incoming food eventually became a logistical challenge. By the evening of July 21, so much had arrived that the CJP posted on X: "India is such a beautiful country with such beautiful people — thanks for sending food for protesters. We are so overwhelmed. BUT for today, we have received more than enough food — please don't send any more!"

Two days later, their Instagram account shared a post redirecting support toward more practical supplies: gloves, brooms, water bottles, and dustbins.

The Diaspora Connection

For Indians living abroad, the delivery apps have offered a way to participate in a protest movement they cannot physically join. Orders placed from overseas — confirmed by multiple delivery partners at Jantar Mantar — highlight how diaspora communities are using digital platforms to stay connected to civic movements at home.

"We also feel deeply connected to this protest. We support it wholeheartedly."

— Neg Singh, delivery rider who made 19 trips to the protest site

The delivery partners themselves have become part of the story. Several riders told reporters they identified with the students' struggles — limited job opportunities had pushed many of them into gig work. Every order they carried to a protest site carried a personal resonance.

What's Next

The CJP protests in Delhi were called off after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on July 25 and the government agreed to demands including exam reforms and compensation for families of students who died by suicide over the leak scandal. India's Central Bureau of Investigation has since filed charges against 13 people connected to the NEET paper leak, and the Supreme Court has ordered no coercive action against protesters.

But exam-related protests continue in Jharkhand and other states, and the food delivery solidarity model appears to have become a lasting feature of India's protest toolkit. Neither Swiggy nor Zomato responded to Outlook Business's requests for comment on the trend.
